Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which educational institution did Aharon Adibekjan attend?
Document 1: Title: The Academic Odyssey of Aharon Adibekjan: A Life of Sociological Inquiry

In the heart of Yerevan, Armenia, a young Aharon Adibekjan embarked on a journey that would shape his future as a renowned sociologist. The year was 1960, and Aharon, with an insatiable thirst for knowledge, enrolled in the National Polytechnic University of Armenia, a prestigious institution that would lay the foundation for his illustrious career. As Aharon navigated the university's corridors, he was drawn to the vibrant atmosphere of intellectual curiosity that permeated the campus. The National Polytechnic University of Armenia, founded in 1933, had established itself as a hub for academic excellence, attracting talented students from across the country. Aharon's decision to attend this esteemed institution was a testament to his commitment to pursuing a rigorous education in the field of sociology. During his time at the university, Aharon was exposed to a diverse range of courses that delved into the intricacies of human behavior, social structures, and cultural dynamics. He was particularly drawn to the works of prominent sociologists, such as Émile Durkheim and Max Weber, whose theories on social solidarity and bureaucracy resonated deeply with him. Aharon's academic pursuits were guided by a passion for understanding the complexities of Armenian society, which had been shaped by centuries of cultural and historical influences. One of Aharon's most influential professors at the National Polytechnic University of Armenia was Dr. Hmayak Yessayan, a distinguished sociologist in his own right. Dr. Yessayan's lectures on social theory and methodology not only deepened Aharon's understanding of the subject matter but also instilled in him a critical thinking approach that would serve him well throughout his career. Aharon's academic performance was exemplary, earning him recognition as one of the top students in his cohort. Upon graduating from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia in 1965, Aharon was well-equipped to tackle the challenges of a rapidly changing Armenian society. His academic foundation, built on the principles of sociological inquiry, enabled him to navigate the complexities of social research, policy analysis, and community engagement. Aharon's subsequent career, marked by numerous publications, research projects, and academic appointments, was a testament to the strong educational foundation he had established at the National Polytechnic University of Armenia.
Document 2: As the sun set over the ancient streets of Santiago de Compostela, a young Aharon Adibekjan strolled through the historic campus of the university, his eyes drinking in the rich history that seemed to seep from every stone. It was the early 1960s, and the Armenian sociologist, still in his early twenties, had just arrived in Spain, eager to expand his knowledge and broaden his horizons. Professor Elena García, a renowned expert in social anthropology, had taken a particular interest in Aharon's work and had invited him to attend a semester-long program at the University of Santiago de Compostela. Aharon was thrilled at the opportunity to learn from the best and to immerse himself in the vibrant cultural landscape of Galicia. As he walked through the cloistered quadrangles, Aharon couldn't help but feel a sense of awe at the university's storied past. Founded in the 16th century, the institution had played host to some of the greatest minds in Spanish history, and Aharon felt honored to be following in their footsteps. One afternoon, while browsing through the shelves of the university library, Aharon stumbled upon a dusty old tome titled "The Social Fabric of Rural Galicia." The author, a certain Dr. Francisco Suárez, had written extensively on the subject of rural communities in the region, and Aharon was fascinated by the parallels he drew between the social structures of Galicia and those of his native Armenia. Intrigued, Aharon decided to track down Dr. Suárez, hoping to engage in a discussion about his work. After inquiring with the librarian, he was directed to a small café on the outskirts of the campus, where he found the elderly professor sipping a cup of strong coffee and puffing on a pipe. The two men struck up a conversation that would last for hours, delving deep into the intricacies of social theory and the nuances of cultural identity. Aharon was struck by Dr. Suárez's warmth and generosity, and the professor, in turn, was impressed by the young Armenian's keen intellect and passion for his work. As the semester drew to a close, Aharon reflected on the incredible experiences he had had at the University of Santiago de Compostela. From the stimulating lectures to the lively debates in the student union, he had felt his mind expand in ways he never thought possible.
